tracks.title: Geometry
tracks.subtitle: Think in shapes. Prove with confidence.
tracks.description: Build a visual and logical foundation: angles, proof, congruence, similarity, circles and three-dimensional measurement.

tracks.title: Algebra 2
tracks.subtitle: Find the patterns behind the numbers.
tracks.description: Go deeper into functions, quadratics, polynomials, radicals, exponentials and logarithms, with plenty of applied modeling.

tracks.title: Math Bridge
tracks.subtitle: Go beyond the classroom.
tracks.description: Extend your course with statistics, probability, the unit circle and precalculus skills used in IB MYP and honors pathways.

chapters.title: Foundations & Proof
chapters.description: Learn the vocabulary and logic that turn a drawing into a mathematical argument.

chapters.title: Triangles & Congruence
chapters.description: Master triangle rules and justify when two triangles are exactly the same shape and size.

chapters.title: Similarity & Right-Triangle Trigonometry
chapters.description: Connect scale factors, right-triangle distances and sine, cosine and tangent.

chapters.title: Polygons & Circles
chapters.description: Use shape properties and circle geometry to solve visual and numerical problems.

chapters.title: Area, Surface Area & Volume
chapters.description: Model two-dimensional and three-dimensional figures with the right units and formulas.

chapters.title: Functions & Graphs
chapters.description: Understand the language of functions before studying their families.

chapters.title: Quadratics & Complex Numbers
chapters.description: Solve second-degree equations and extend arithmetic to non-real solutions.

chapters.title: Polynomial Functions
chapters.description: Analyze higher-degree expressions and their factor/graph relationships.

chapters.title: Rational & Radical Expressions
chapters.description: Work safely with fractions involving variables and equations involving square roots.

chapters.title: Exponents, Logs & Sequences
chapters.description: Model repeated multiplication, undo exponentiation and recognize iterative patterns.

chapters.title: Statistics & Probability
chapters.description: Make sense of data and calculate the likelihood of outcomes.

chapters.title: Unit Circle & Trigonometric Laws
chapters.description: Extend right-triangle trigonometry to all angles and non-right triangles.

chapters.title: Precalculus Function Skills
chapters.description: Read challenging function restrictions and transform formulas into models.

lessons.title: Points, Lines & Planes
lessons.summary: Geometry starts by describing locations and the objects connecting them. A point has no size; a line extends forever in both directions; a plane is a flat surface extending without end.
ideas: Name a point with a capital letter, and a line using two points on it.
Two distinct points determine exactly one line; three noncollinear points determine exactly one plane.
Segments have two endpoints, while rays begin at one point and continue forever in one direction.
formulas: Segment length on a number line = ∣b − a∣

workedExample.prompt: Points A and B are at −3 and 7 on a number line. Find the length and midpoint of AB.
steps: A segment is finite, even though its supporting line goes on forever.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not confuse a segment with a full line; the segment has endpoints.
lessons.realWorld: Map coordinates, architectural diagrams and computer graphics all rely on points and segments.

lessons.title: Angles & Parallel Lines
lessons.summary: Angles measure a turn between two rays. Parallel lines intersected by a transversal create repeating angle patterns.
ideas: Vertical angles are equal; a linear pair sums to 180°.
Corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal when the lines are parallel.
Same-side interior angles are supplementary: their measures add to 180°.

workedExample.prompt: One alternate interior angle measures 68°. Find the matching angle when the lines are parallel.
steps: Identify the pair as alternate interior angles.
Parallel lines make alternate interior angles congruent.

lessons.commonMistake: Adjacent does not always mean equal; check whether the angles are vertical, corresponding or supplementary.
lessons.realWorld: Street grids and stair railings use parallel-line angle reasoning.

lessons.title: Logic & Two-Column Proofs
lessons.summary: A proof is a chain of statements, each supported by a definition, postulate or theorem. The goal is to explain why a result must be true.
ideas: A conditional statement has hypothesis P and conclusion Q: if P, then Q.
Modus ponens says P and (P → Q) together imply Q.
In a two-column proof, the left column gives statements and the right column gives reasons.
formulas: A = B, B = C ⟹ A = C

workedExample.prompt: Given AB = CD and CD = EF, prove AB = EF.
steps: Use the transitive property of equality: AB = EF.

lessons.commonMistake: A drawing is not proof; properties must follow from stated facts.
lessons.realWorld: Formal reasoning supports coding, science experiments and persuasive arguments.

lessons.title: Triangle Angle Relationships
lessons.summary: The three interior angles of any triangle add to 180°. Exterior angles encode the two remote interior angles.
ideas: Classify triangles as acute, right or obtuse by their angles.
The interior angle sum is 180° for every Euclidean triangle.
An exterior angle equals the sum of its two non-adjacent interior angles.
formulas: Exterior angle = remote angle 1 + remote angle 2

workedExample.prompt: A triangle has angles 42° and 63°. Find its third angle.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not add 360°; that is the angle sum for a quadrilateral.
lessons.realWorld: Surveyors use triangle-angle relationships to find inaccessible positions.

lessons.title: Triangle Congruence
lessons.summary: Congruent triangles match in every side and angle. You rarely need all six measurements to prove it.
ideas: SSS uses three pairs of matching sides.
SAS uses two sides and the included angle; ASA and AAS use corresponding angles and a side.
AAA proves similarity, not congruence; SSA is not a general congruence criterion.
formulas: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL (right triangles)
CPCTC: corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent

workedExample.prompt: Two triangles have matching sides 5, 7 and 9. What makes them congruent?
steps: List three pairs of matching side lengths.
The corresponding angles must also match.

lessons.commonMistake: SAS requires the INCLUDED angle, not any angle.
lessons.realWorld: Engineers check congruent supports to ensure repeated components fit.

lessons.title: Triangle Inequality & Isosceles Triangles
lessons.summary: Not every three lengths can create a triangle. Equal sides also reveal information about angles.
ideas: The sum of any two side lengths must be greater than the third.
For ordered side lengths a ≤ b ≤ c, checking a + b > c is enough.
In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite equal sides are equal.

workedExample.prompt: Can lengths 4, 6 and 9 form a triangle?
steps: Find the two shorter lengths: 4 and 6.

lessons.commonMistake: Equality is not enough: 4 + 5 = 9 creates a straight segment, not a triangle.
lessons.realWorld: Construction crews use bracing triangles because valid, rigid shapes matter.

lessons.title: Similarity & Scale Factor
lessons.summary: Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional matching side lengths. The scale factor changes distances but not shape.
ideas: AA is enough to show two triangles are similar.
Match corresponding sides in the same order when writing proportions.
Perimeter scales by k, while area scales by k².

workedExample.prompt: A triangle with side 6 is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. Find the new side.
steps: Other corresponding sides use the same factor.

lessons.commonMistake: Area does not scale by k; it scales by k².
lessons.realWorld: Maps, blueprints and photo enlargements are all similarity models.

lessons.title: Pythagorean Theorem
lessons.summary: A right triangle links its legs and hypotenuse through a beautiful square-area relationship.
ideas: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.
For legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c².
Common triples include 3-4-5, 5-12-13 and scaled copies.

workedExample.prompt: A ladder reaches 12 feet up a wall and its foot is 5 feet away. How long is it?
steps: Identify the ladder as the hypotenuse.
Take the positive root: c = 13 feet.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not treat the hypotenuse as a leg; it must be c.
lessons.realWorld: Navigation, screens and building diagonals all use right-triangle distance.

lessons.title: Sine, Cosine & Tangent
lessons.summary: Trigonometric ratios connect an acute angle to lengths in a right triangle. You can find missing sides without knowing every angle.
ideas: Relative to angle θ, identify opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse.
Sine is opposite/hypotenuse; cosine is adjacent/hypotenuse.
Tangent is opposite/adjacent; use inverse trig to find an angle.

workedExample.prompt: A right triangle has opposite side 3 and hypotenuse 5 relative to θ. Find sin θ.

lessons.commonMistake: Opposite and adjacent depend on the angle you choose.
lessons.realWorld: Measure heights of trees or slopes of ramps from safe distances.

lessons.title: Quadrilaterals & Polygons
lessons.summary: Polygons are closed figures of straight line segments. Their interior angle sums depend only on the number of sides.
ideas: A quadrilateral has interior angle sum 360°.
Parallelograms have opposite sides parallel and equal, and opposite angles equal.
Rectangles have four right angles; rhombi have four equal sides; squares have both properties.

workedExample.prompt: Find the sum of interior angles of a hexagon.

lessons.commonMistake: A square is a rectangle and a rhombus, not a completely unrelated shape.
lessons.realWorld: Floor tiles and roof trusses use polygon properties.

lessons.title: Chords, Tangents & Circle Angles
lessons.summary: Circle angles encode arcs. Central angles and inscribed angles that intercept the same arc follow a 2-to-1 relationship.
ideas: A central angle has its vertex at the circle center.
An inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle and measures half its intercepted arc.
A radius to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent line.

workedExample.prompt: An inscribed angle intercepts an arc measuring 110°. Find the angle.
steps: An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not halve the arc for a central angle: central angle and arc have equal measures.
lessons.realWorld: Rotating parts and curved roadway designs depend on circular angles.

lessons.title: Arc Length & Sector Area
lessons.summary: A sector is a slice of a circle. Its arc length and area are fractions of the full circle determined by the central angle.
ideas: Use degree fractions when the central angle is in degrees.
Circumference is 2πr, while circle area is πr².
For radian measure θ, arc length simplifies to rθ.

workedExample.prompt: Find the arc length of a 90° sector in a circle of radius 8.
steps: A 90° arc is one quarter of a full turn.

lessons.commonMistake: Arc length has distance units; sector area has square units.
lessons.realWorld: Pizza portions, gears and irrigation sprinklers form sectors.

lessons.title: Perimeter & Area
lessons.summary: Perimeter measures distance around a figure; area counts the unit squares within it.
ideas: Rectangle perimeter adds all four sides; its area multiplies length and width.
Triangle area uses half the base times the perpendicular height.
Circle circumference and area use π and radius.

workedExample.prompt: A rectangular garden is 8 meters by 5 meters. Find its area and perimeter.

lessons.commonMistake: The slanted side of a triangle is not always its height.
lessons.realWorld: Garden design and flooring estimates require area and perimeter.

lessons.title: Surface Area of Solids
lessons.summary: Surface area adds the areas of all exposed faces of a solid. Net diagrams help make sure no face is missed.
ideas: A rectangular prism has three pairs of equal opposing faces.
A cylinder has two circles and one curved lateral surface.
For pyramids and cones, distinguish slant height from vertical height.

workedExample.prompt: Find the surface area of a box measuring 2 by 3 by 4.
steps: Compute the three pair areas: 2×3, 2×4 and 3×4.
Double for opposite faces: 52 square units.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not confuse slant height with perpendicular height.
lessons.realWorld: Packaging designers minimize material while covering every face.

lessons.title: Volume of Solids
lessons.summary: Volume measures the space inside a three-dimensional figure. Recognize the cross-sectional base area first.
ideas: A prism or cylinder volume equals base area × height.
Pyramids and cones have one-third the volume of their matching prism or cylinder.
A sphere volume is four-thirds π times radius cubed.

workedExample.prompt: Find the volume of a cylinder of radius 3 and height 5.

lessons.commonMistake: Volume uses cubic units, not square units.
lessons.realWorld: Water tanks and storage containers are modeled by volume.

lessons.title: Function Notation & Evaluation
lessons.summary: A function assigns exactly one output to each input. Function notation makes it easy to describe and evaluate rules.
ideas: f(x) means the output when input x is given; it is not multiplication f×x.
A vertical line test checks whether a graph is a function.
Inputs form the domain; resulting outputs form the range.

workedExample.prompt: Given f(x) = 3x − 2, find f(5).

lessons.commonMistake: Substitute into the entire expression before simplifying.
lessons.realWorld: Cost, distance and temperature rules can all be expressed as functions.

lessons.title: Graph Transformations
lessons.summary: Transformations move or reshape a parent graph while preserving recognizable patterns.
ideas: Adding outside the function shifts the graph vertically.
Replacing x by (x−h) shifts the graph RIGHT h units.
A negative outside the function reflects it over the x-axis.

workedExample.prompt: Find the vertex of y = (x − 4)² + 3.

lessons.commonMistake: Horizontal shifts seem backwards: (x−4) means right 4.
lessons.realWorld: Transform graphs to model growth, projectile paths and signals.

lessons.title: Composite Functions
lessons.summary: Composition applies one function to the output of another. Order matters because f(g(x)) usually differs from g(f(x)).
ideas: Compute the inside function first.
Use its output as the next function input.
For composition, check that the inside output belongs to the outer domain.

workedExample.prompt: If f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x², find f(g(3)).
steps: Use 9 as input to f: f(9)=2×9+1.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not multiply f and g; the circle notation means compose.
lessons.realWorld: Multi-stage pricing and unit conversion are function compositions.

lessons.title: Factoring Quadratics
lessons.summary: Factoring expresses a quadratic as a product of binomials, which can reveal its roots quickly.
ideas: For x²+bx+c, find numbers that sum to b and multiply to c.
The zero-product property says AB=0 implies A=0 or B=0.
Always check the expression is equal to zero before reading roots.
formulas: x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q), p+q=b, pq=c

workedExample.prompt: Factor x² + 7x + 12 and solve x²+7x+12=0.

lessons.commonMistake: Factoring an expression and solving an equation are different tasks.
lessons.realWorld: Quadratic roots predict when trajectories reach ground level.

lessons.title: Quadratic Formula & Discriminant
lessons.summary: The quadratic formula solves any equation ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0. The discriminant tells you what sort of roots to expect.
ideas: First identify a, b and c with the equation written as zero.
The discriminant D=b²−4ac determines the number of real roots.
D>0 gives two distinct real roots, D=0 one repeated root, D<0 no real roots.

workedExample.prompt: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0.

lessons.commonMistake: The denominator is 2a for the WHOLE numerator.
lessons.realWorld: Projectile motion and revenue optimization involve quadratic models.

lessons.title: Introduction to Complex Numbers
lessons.summary: Complex numbers extend real arithmetic using i, defined so i²=−1. They let us describe quadratic roots that are not real.
ideas: A complex number has real part a and imaginary part b in a+bi.
Add real parts together and imaginary parts together.
Powers of i repeat every four steps: i, −1, −i, 1.

workedExample.prompt: Simplify (3+2i)+(4−5i).

lessons.commonMistake: i is not the same as −1; i² equals −1.
lessons.realWorld: Electrical engineering uses complex numbers to model alternating currents.

lessons.title: Adding & Multiplying Polynomials
lessons.summary: Polynomial operations combine like powers of x and use distribution to multiply every relevant term.
ideas: Like terms have identical variable powers.
When multiplying monomials, add their exponents.
Multiply binomials with distribution, then combine like terms.

workedExample.prompt: Expand (x+3)(x+5).

lessons.commonMistake: Do not add exponents when adding terms; only combine like powers.
lessons.realWorld: Polynomial expressions model production and geometry relationships.

lessons.title: Synthetic Division & Factor Theorem
lessons.summary: Division reveals whether a linear expression is a polynomial factor. Synthetic division is a compact method for x−c divisors.
ideas: The Remainder Theorem says the remainder upon dividing P(x) by x−c equals P(c).
If P(c)=0, then x−c is a factor.
Write missing polynomial powers as zero coefficients before synthetic division.

workedExample.prompt: For P(x)=x²−5x+6, is x−2 a factor?

lessons.commonMistake: For a divisor x+3, synthetic input c is −3, not +3.
lessons.realWorld: Factor tests help identify roots of higher-degree models.

lessons.title: End Behavior & Turning Points
lessons.summary: A polynomial’s leading term controls how its graph behaves far left and far right.
ideas: Even-degree polynomials point the same way at both ends.
Odd-degree polynomials point in opposite directions.
A positive leading coefficient makes the right end point up; a negative one makes it point down.
formulas: Maximum turning points for degree n: n−1

workedExample.prompt: Describe the right-end behavior of f(x)=−2x³+5x+1.
steps: Odd degree and negative coefficient give a falling right end.

lessons.commonMistake: Lower-degree terms do not control end behavior.
lessons.realWorld: End behavior helps interpret long-range growth models.

lessons.title: Simplifying Rational Expressions
lessons.summary: Rational expressions are fractions of polynomials. Factoring often exposes common factors that can be canceled.
ideas: Factor the numerator and denominator before canceling.
Only cancel common MULTIPLICATIVE factors, never terms separated by + or −.
Excluded inputs make the original denominator equal zero, even if a factor cancels.

workedExample.prompt: Simplify (x²−16)/(x−4).
steps: The result is x+4, with x≠4.

lessons.commonMistake: (x+2)/x does not simplify to 2; never cancel across addition.
lessons.realWorld: Rates, mixture formulas and rational models use variable fractions.

lessons.title: Radical Expressions & Equations
lessons.summary: Radicals reverse powers, but squaring both sides can introduce answers that do not satisfy the starting equation.
ideas: √x is the nonnegative principal square root.
Isolate the radical before squaring both sides.
Substitute candidate solutions into the ORIGINAL equation to reject extraneous roots.

workedExample.prompt: Solve √(x+5)=4.

lessons.commonMistake: Squaring can add invalid solutions; always check.
lessons.realWorld: Distance and energy formulas often contain square roots.

lessons.title: Rational Graphs & Asymptotes
lessons.summary: A rational function can approach a line without touching it. Zeros of denominators and polynomial degrees predict its behavior.
ideas: A vertical asymptote often occurs where a reduced denominator is zero.
If numerator degree is less than denominator degree, horizontal asymptote is y=0.
If degrees are equal, the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of leading coefficients.
formulas: Equal degrees: HA y = leading coefficient ratio

workedExample.prompt: Find the vertical asymptote of f(x)=3/(x−5)+2.
steps: This is the vertical asymptote; y=2 is horizontal.

lessons.commonMistake: A canceled denominator factor creates a hole, not necessarily a vertical asymptote.
lessons.realWorld: Rational graphs describe saturation and inverse-distance behavior.

lessons.title: Exponential Growth & Decay
lessons.summary: Exponential models multiply by the same factor over equal time intervals. This is different from adding a fixed amount.
ideas: In y=a·bᵗ, a is the initial amount and b is the growth/decay factor.
For a growth rate r, b=1+r; for decay rate r, b=1−r.
Equal percentage change creates exponential rather than linear growth.

workedExample.prompt: A population of 200 grows by 10% per year. Find the count after two years.

lessons.commonMistake: 10% growth means multiply by 1.10, not add 10 each year.
lessons.realWorld: Population, compound interest and bacterial growth are exponential.

lessons.title: Logarithms & Inverse Operations
lessons.summary: A logarithm asks for the exponent required to reach a number. It is the inverse of exponentiation.
ideas: log_b(x)=y means bʸ=x, with b>0 and b≠1.
The argument of a real logarithm must be positive.
Product, quotient and power rules simplify logarithmic expressions.

workedExample.prompt: Evaluate log₂(32).

lessons.commonMistake: log(a+b) is NOT log a + log b.
lessons.realWorld: The Richter-like scales and sound intensity use logarithmic scales.

lessons.title: Arithmetic & Geometric Sequences
lessons.summary: Sequences organize numbers by position. Arithmetic sequences add a constant; geometric sequences multiply by a constant.
ideas: Arithmetic sequences have common difference d.
Geometric sequences have common ratio r.
For finite sums, use the number of terms and the right formula.

workedExample.prompt: Find term 6 of the arithmetic sequence 4, 7, 10, …
steps: The first term is 4 and common difference is 3.

lessons.commonMistake: The nth term uses n−1 jumps from the first term.
lessons.realWorld: Savings plans and repeated patterns can be modeled as sequences.

lessons.title: Mean, Median & Standard Deviation
lessons.summary: Summary measures describe the center and spread of a data set. Different measures answer different questions.
ideas: Mean is the arithmetic average; median is the middle after sorting.
Range is maximum minus minimum; outliers influence mean more than median.
Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean in the same units as data.

workedExample.prompt: Find the mean and range of 3, 5, 7, 9.

lessons.commonMistake: The median cannot be identified reliably without sorting first.
lessons.realWorld: Teams use statistics to evaluate performance and compare populations.

lessons.title: Permutations & Combinations
lessons.summary: Counting techniques avoid writing every possible arrangement. The key question is whether order matters.
ideas: Use the multiplication principle for independent stages.
Permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations count unordered selections.
Factorial n! multiplies every positive integer up to n, and 0!=1.

workedExample.prompt: How many ways can you choose 2 captains from 5 students when order does not matter?
steps: This is a combination because the selected pair has no order.

lessons.commonMistake: A team selection uses combinations; assigning president and vice president uses permutations.
lessons.realWorld: Event planning and probability calculations depend on counting.

lessons.title: Conditional Probability
lessons.summary: Conditional probability revises the sample space using information you already know.
ideas: P(A∣B) means probability of A given B happened.
For equally likely outcomes, compare the overlap with the size of B.
Independent events satisfy P(A∣B)=P(A), when P(B)>0.

workedExample.prompt: From 12 students, 5 play soccer, and 3 of those 5 also play chess. Find P(chess | soccer).
steps: Restrict attention to the 5 soccer players.
Count the 3 who also play chess.

lessons.commonMistake: The denominator for P(A∣B) is the size/probability of B, not the entire group.
lessons.realWorld: Medical testing and everyday risk estimates use conditional probability.

lessons.title: Radian Measure & Unit Circle
lessons.summary: The unit circle turns trigonometry into coordinates, making sine and cosine meaningful for any rotation.
ideas: A full turn is 2π radians or 360°.
At angle θ on the unit circle, the coordinate is (cos θ, sin θ).
Quadrant signs determine whether sine and cosine are positive or negative.
formulas: Unit circle point = (cos θ, sin θ)

workedExample.prompt: Convert 150° to radians.

lessons.commonMistake: Radians are not degrees; use the correct calculator mode.
lessons.realWorld: Waves, rotations and periodic motion use radians.

lessons.title: Law of Sines
lessons.summary: The Law of Sines relates side lengths to the sines of their opposite angles in any triangle.
ideas: Use the law when you know a side and its opposite angle.
Match lowercase side a to uppercase opposite angle A.
The SSA case can sometimes produce two possible triangles.
formulas: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C

workedExample.prompt: If side a=10 opposite A=30°, find side b opposite B=90°.

lessons.commonMistake: Never pair a side with an angle that is not opposite it.
lessons.realWorld: Triangulation can find distances between landmarks.

lessons.title: Law of Cosines
lessons.summary: The Law of Cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem to triangles without a right angle.
ideas: Use it with two sides and the included angle (SAS), or all three sides (SSS).
The cosine correction accounts for the included angle.
At 90°, cos90°=0, so it becomes the Pythagorean theorem.

workedExample.prompt: Two sides of a triangle are 5 and 7 with included angle 60°. Find the opposite side.

lessons.commonMistake: The angle must be between the two provided sides for SAS use.
lessons.realWorld: Navigation uses this rule to estimate distance between two travel legs.

lessons.title: Domain, Range & Restrictions
lessons.summary: The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of attained outputs. Algebraic operations can restrict inputs.
ideas: A real square-root expression requires its radicand to be nonnegative.
A denominator cannot equal zero.
For quadratics in vertex form, the vertex helps identify the range.

workedExample.prompt: Find the real domain of f(x)=√(x−4).
steps: Solve the inequality to get x≥4.

lessons.commonMistake: A rational hole can remain excluded even if you cancel a factor.
lessons.realWorld: Domain restrictions keep scientific models physically meaningful.

lessons.title: Inverse Functions
lessons.summary: An inverse reverses what a one-to-one function does. Inputs and outputs exchange places.
ideas: A function needs to be one-to-one on its domain to have an inverse function.
To find an inverse, write y=f(x), swap x and y, then solve for y.
The graph of the inverse reflects across y=x.

workedExample.prompt: Find the inverse of f(x)=3x+6.
steps: Write y=3x+6 and swap x,y: x=3y+6.

lessons.commonMistake: f⁻¹(x) means inverse function, not 1/f(x).
lessons.realWorld: Currency conversion and encoding/decoding use inverse relationships.

lessons.title: Function Modeling & Composition
lessons.summary: Applied problems rarely announce the function to use. First identify relationships, inputs, units and restrictions.
ideas: Translate a story into a rule and define what x represents.
Check units and sensible domain restrictions.
To connect two processes, compose their functions in the right order.

workedExample.prompt: A bike rental charges $8 plus $3 per hour. Find the cost for 5 hours.

lessons.commonMistake: Always include the fixed starting cost; it is the y-intercept.
lessons.realWorld: Budgeting, transportation and pricing provide natural function models.
